Part 1 of 7

Tension and Compression

Every bridge has one job: carry a load across a gap without falling down.

The load is the weight of everything the bridge holds up: the cars, the people, and the bridge itself. Gravity pulls all that weight down. To stay up, a bridge passes that weight through its parts and down into the ground at each end.

As the weight travels, every part of the bridge gets pushed or pulled. Engineers call these two forces compression and tension.

Gravity is the big one

Gravity is the biggest force a bridge has to fight. A building stands on solid ground, but a bridge stretches across empty space, and empty space can't hold anything up. The longer and heavier the bridge, the harder its job.

Engineers split the load into two kinds:

Dead loadThe bridge's own weight. It's always there.
Live loadThings that come and go: cars, trucks, trains, and people. As they cross, the bridge bends a tiny bit, then springs back.

The parts of a bridge

The part of a bridge you drive or walk on is called the deck. The distance the bridge crosses from one support to the next is its span. The longer the span, the more weight sits out over empty space, and the harder the bridge has to work.

Bridges are built from two basic kinds of pieces. A beam is a long, stiff piece that lies flat, like the deck or the top and bottom of a truss. A column is a long, stiff piece that stands up straight and holds things up from below. Beams usually bend under weight, so one side gets squeezed and the other gets stretched. Columns mostly get squeezed, which is why long, thin columns can buckle.

Compression

A squeezing force. It pushes on a part from both ends and makes it shorter.

Examples: your legs when you stand. A column holding up a roof.

Watch out: when something long and thin is squeezed, it bends sideways and can snap. This is called buckling. See it below.

Tension

A stretching force. It pulls on a part from both ends and makes it longer.

Examples: a rope in tug-of-war. A guitar string.

Watch out: when a part is pulled too hard, it snaps or pulls loose at the joint.

What buckling looks like

Squeeze the ends of a long, thin metal beam and it doesn't just get shorter. It bows out to the side. Push harder and it bends permanently or snaps. A short, thick beam squeezed the same way stays straight.

Both forces at once

Put weight on the middle of a metal beam and it bends. The top is squeezed together and the bottom is stretched apart, at the same time.

Other forces engineers plan for

Weight isn't the only thing pushing on a bridge. Engineers also plan for:

WindPushes the bridge sideways and can make it sway or twist. Many modern bridges are shaped so wind slips past.
WaterRivers, tides, and waves push against the supports. Supports are often shaped so water flows smoothly around them.
EarthquakesShake the whole bridge. Engineers add parts called dampers that soak up the shaking.
Heat and coldSteel and concrete expand (get a little bigger) when hot and shrink when cold. Bridges have small gaps so the parts have room to move.

Different materials, different strengths

Stone, concreteStrong when squeezed. Cracks when stretched.
SteelStrong when squeezed and when stretched.
Rope, cableOnly works in tension. You can't push with a rope.

Part 2 of 7

Truss Bridges

A truss bridge is a beam bridge made stronger with a frame of triangles.

The triangles share the load, so the bridge can be light and still very strong. That's why trusses are one of the most common bridge designs. You'll see them carrying trains, cars, and people on foot.

In the 1800s, railroad companies built thousands of truss bridges so trains could cross rivers and valleys. Trains are very heavy, and trusses let builders make long, strong bridges out of wood and iron without using too much material.

How it works

When weight presses down, a truss acts like the bending beam from Part 1:

  • The top beam is squeezed: compression.
  • The bottom beam is stretched: tension.
  • The diagonals are mixed. Some are squeezed and some are stretched, depending on which way they slant.

How the triangles share the load

When a truck drives onto a truss bridge, its weight presses down on the deck. The deck passes that weight to the joints, the spots where the parts of the truss meet. At each joint, the weight splits between all the parts connected there, and each part passes its share along to the next joint.

Here's the clever part: each piece of a truss only has to push or pull along its length. A piece of steel or wood is much stronger when you push or pull it end to end than when you try to bend it in the middle. A truss turns one big bending problem into lots of small push and pull jobs.

Road on top, or road through?

Some truss bridges carry the road on top of the frame. This is called a deck truss. Others carry the road along the bottom, so cars drive right through the frame. This is called a through truss. Both work the same way. Engineers choose based on how much room there is above and below the bridge.

Three common trusses

Engineers arrange the triangles in different patterns. The slant of the diagonals decides whether they're squeezed or stretched.

Quick facts

Good atStrong but light. Uses little material.
Weak spotLots of joints to build and check. A weak joint can bring the whole bridge down.
Real examplesQueensboro Bridge, New York City. Astoria–Megler Bridge, between Oregon and Washington. Forth Bridge, Scotland.
Fun fact: a bridge that curls upThe Rolling Bridge in London is a small walking bridge made of 8 triangle-shaped sections. When it's flat, it works like a truss. When a boat needs to pass, it curls up into a circle.

Part 3 of 7

Arch Bridges

An arch bridge carries weight along a curve.

When weight presses down on an arch, the whole curve gets squeezed. It pushes the load out along the curve, down to the ground at each end. Almost the whole arch is in compression.

Stone arches and the keystone

The ancient Romans built arches out of stone, which is strong when squeezed. Some of their arch bridges are still standing after about 2,000 years.

A stone arch is made of wedge-shaped stones, each a little wider at the top than the bottom. The last stone goes in at the very top. It's called the keystone. The stones on each side squeeze it tight, and it locks the whole arch in place.

Until the keystone is in, the arch can't hold itself up. So builders first made a curved wooden frame, set the stones on top of it, and dropped in the keystone last. Then they took the frame away, and the arch stood on its own.

Arches today

Today, many arches are built from steel or concrete, which lets them stretch much farther. When the New River Gorge Bridge in West Virginia opened in 1977, it was the longest single-span steel arch bridge in the world.

Some arch bridges carry the road on top of the arch, like the New River Gorge Bridge. Others have the road running through the middle, hanging from the arch above. The Sydney Harbour Bridge in Australia works this way. Either way, the arch is squeezed and carries the weight to the supports at each end.

The ends push out

The bottom ends of an arch push down and outward. The supports at each end push back. If nothing holds the ends in place, the arch spreads apart and falls.

The tied arch

Some arch bridges tie their two ends together with the road deck. Now the ends can't spread apart. The arch is still squeezed, but the deck tying it together is stretched, in tension.

When engineers use a tied archA plain arch needs solid rock or strong ground at each end to push against. When the ground can't push back hard enough, engineers tie the ends together instead.

Quick facts

Good atVery strong. Can last a long time. Can be built from stone.
Weak spotNeeds strong supports at the ends. Hard to build: the arch can't hold itself up until both halves meet in the middle.
Real examplesHell Gate Bridge, New York City. New River Gorge Bridge, West Virginia. Sydney Harbour Bridge, Australia.

Part 4 of 7

Why Triangles Are Strong

A triangle can't change shape unless one of its sides changes length.

Build a square from four sticks with loose joints and push on a corner. It leans over into a diamond and collapses. None of its sides got longer or shorter. Only the angles at the corners changed.

Now push on a triangle. To change shape, one of its sides would have to get longer or shorter. So each side gets squeezed or stretched instead, and the triangle holds.

Triangles share the push

When you push on one corner of a triangle, the push splits between the two sides that meet there. One side gets squeezed and the other gets stretched. No single piece has to do all the work.

Every other shape can fold

It isn't just squares. A pentagon, a hexagon, or any shape with more than three sides can fold if its joints can turn. The triangle is the only shape whose angles are locked by the lengths of its sides. That's why engineers break bigger shapes into triangles.

Try it: push the shapes

Pick a direction, then drag the slider to push on each shape. Try both directions. Then add diagonals to the square and hexagon and push again.

The joints matter

A triangle is only strong if its corners hold tight. If a joint slips or pulls apart, the triangle can change shape after all. That's why engineers spend so much time on the connections. On real bridges, the joints are held with bolts, rivets, or welds, and inspectors check them closely.

Where you'll see them

Truss bridges, roof frames, and power line towers are all built from triangles. A bike frame is two triangles joined together. The Eiffel Tower in Paris is a giant lattice of iron triangles. Anywhere something needs to be strong but light, look for triangles.

Part 5 of 7

Bridge Game: Fix It

Your teacher built a bridge that fails. Your job is to fix it.

You'll use Bridge Designer, a free game from the American Society of Civil Engineers. A truck drives across your bridge to test it.

  1. Get the starter bridge.

    Download Starter Bridge.bdc from Google Classroom.

    Or download it here instead:

  2. Open the game.

    ASCE Bridge Designer

  3. Open the starter bridge in the game.

    Click File, then Open…, and pick Starter Bridge.bdc.

  4. Run the load test.

    Watch the truck. The bridge will fail, and the status turns to a red sign.

    Screenshot 1: the failed bridge
  5. Look at the colors.

    During the test, the game colors each part to show whether it's being squeezed or stretched. Check the game's color key. Which parts are squeezed? Which are stretched? Which part broke?

  6. Predict, then fix it.

    Before you change anything, predict what will help. Then add or change parts. Test again. Keep trying until it passes.

  7. Run the test again.

    When the truck makes it across and the status shows a green arrow, take your second screenshot.

    Screenshot 2: the fixed bridge

Game buttons

These are the buttons you'll use most.

Design bridge

Go back to building mode. Use this after a test when you want to change your bridge.

Run test

Drive the truck across your bridge to see if it holds.

Status

Yellow worker: not tested since your last change. Red sign: the bridge failed. Green arrow: the bridge passed!

File menu

Open… opens a bridge file. Save saves your work. Save as… saves a copy with a new name, so you can try a cheaper idea without losing the bridge that works.

Joint (circle)Adds a joint, a connecting point. Click where you want it.
Member (two dots and a line)Adds a member, a bar between two joints. Connect one joint to another.
Select (arrow)Picks a joint or member, so you can change it, like making a member thicker.
Erase (eraser)Deletes the joint or member you click.
Bonus: under $500,000Can you fix the bridge so it passes and costs less than $500,000? The game shows your bridge's cost as you work. Make sure the cost shows in your screenshot, then turn it in on Google Classroom.
Bonus screenshot: passing bridge under $500,000

Part 6 of 7

Bridge Challenge

Design your own bridge that passes the truck test for less than $475,000.

The prize

The 3 cheapest bridges in all of your teacher's classes win a prize.

The rules

  • Start with the challenge file below. It already has the site and the deck set up.
  • Don't change the bridge height or the deck. Everyone uses the same setup, so the prices are fair.
  • Add your own joints (the connecting points) and members (the bars between them).
  • Your bridge must pass the truck test.
  • It must cost less than $475,000. The cheaper, the better.

How to do it

  1. Get the challenge file.

    Download Challenge Bridge.bdc from Google Classroom.

    Or download it here instead:

  2. Open it in the game.

    ASCE Bridge Designer. Click File, then Open…, and pick Challenge Bridge.bdc.

  3. Build your bridge.

    Add joints, then connect them with members. Use what you learned: fill the bridge with triangles. Need help with the buttons? See Game buttons in Part 5.

  4. Test it.

    Run the truck test. If it fails, look at which part broke and make that part stronger.

  5. Make it cheaper.

    Once it passes, check the cost. Then try to bring it down and test again after every change.

  6. Save your bridge often.

    Click File, then Save, so you don't lose your work.

Tips for a cheaper bridgeFewer joints and members usually cost less. Try a different pattern of triangles, like Warren, Pratt, or Howe. Parts that barely get squeezed or stretched during the test might work with a smaller size. Change one thing at a time, then test again.
Turn it in

On Google Classroom, turn in one of these:

  • A screenshot of your bridge passing the truck test, with the cost showing
  • Your saved bridge file

This is separate from your worksheet.
